title: What's the deal with dowsing?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore dowsing (water witching), the practice of using forked sticks, metal rods, pendulums, or maps to locate water, ore, buried bodies, or other hidden things. They trace its origins to 16th-century German mining, its spread to England and France, the 17th-century murder-finding story of Jacques Aymar, Harvard-era dowsing surveys in the 1950s, the American Society of Dowsers, and explanations ranging from magnetism and "exhalations" to ideomotor movement and non-conscious intelligence. They cover scientific tests finding dowsers no better than chance, James Randi's million-dollar challenge, UK water companies still using dowsers, and a closing listener mail segment.

segments.title: Intro and live show plug
segments.summary: Josh plugs upcoming live shows, introduces the topic of dowsing (water witching) and the episode title, and notes they covered it in a book chapter before.

segments.title: Origins of dowsing in German mining
segments.summary: Dowsing is traced to 16th-century Germany and mining, with Georgius Agricola's De re metallica (1530s) mentioning divining rods, its spread to England and France where it was used for water, and early 17th-century use of forked hazel twigs (with peach, rowan, and willow also mentioned), including Robert Boyle's description.

segments.title: Dowsing for bodies, treasure, and the Jacques Aymar murders
segments.summary: Dowsing was used to find treasure, bodies, and property boundaries. Jacques Aymar, a French peasant, supposedly located a murdered woman and then her husband, who fled and was found to be the murderer. Later, Aymar was called to help find killers of a wine shop couple, leading to a confession and accomplices. The hosts discuss skeptical readings and the belief that dowsing is an innate gift.

segments.title: Dowsing in the Nazi era and 1950s Harvard studies
segments.summary: Eighteenth-century science reduced dowsing's role in mining. Nazis, including Himmler, used dowsing for explosives, water, and gold. In the 1950s, Harvard sociologists Raymond Hyman and Elizabeth Cohen surveyed agricultural extension agents, finding about 35 dowsers per 100,000 people in rural areas, and that most agents thought it was bunk while others were open-minded; people used dowsers because alternatives were lacking.

segments.title: Ivan Vogt study and the American Society of Dowsers
segments.summary: Ivan Vogt studied dowsing in Homestead, New Mexico, classifying it as folk magic and finding it common in rural agriculture, with belief persisting among educated people where water was scarce. Vogt and Linda Barrett later studied urban dowsers. The American Society of Dowsers, founded in Vermont in the early 1960s, still has chapters worldwide.

segments.title: Break and banter
segments.summary: Short break with lighthearted banter about urban dowsers as a band name and music genre.

segments.title: Dowsing techniques: rods, L-rods, pendulums, and information dowsing
segments.summary: The hosts describe holding Y-shaped rods, L-shaped coat-hanger rods that cross, and pendulums (swinging forward/back for yes, side to side for no). They describe information dowsing as a form of fortune telling and note that women are common dowsers today despite the 1950s survey.

segments.title: Map dowsing and Robert Ader's pamphlet
segments.summary: Map dowsing uses a pendulum or pencil over a map. Robert Ader's pamphlet on the American Society of Dowsers website describes searching for water on the Moon and Bigfoot graves, and an anecdote where the pencil pointed at the Moon until the question was reworded to ask for the location on the map.

segments.title: Explanations: magnetism, breath of metals, and Valmont's particles
segments.summary: Early explanations included magnetism and Johann Thölde (Basilius Valentinus)'s idea that metals breathe out a rising breath. In 1693, Abbé Louis Lazare de Vallemont wrote that particles from water, treasure, or bodies enter the body through pores; he called them 'larvae' (Boyle's effluvia). Later 19th-20th century French priests linked dowsing to radiation, and others proposed electricity, magnetism, ESP, or divine conduit explanations.

segments.title: Ideomotor movement, non-conscious intelligence, and the Ouija board study
segments.summary: Hosts discuss ideomotor movements as a modern explanation, the difference between dowsers picking up on vegetation subconsciously versus water emanations triggering muscles, and a University of British Columbia study by Hélène Giroux finding Ouija-board use improved answers, suggesting non-conscious intelligence.

segments.title: Scientific testing, James Randi challenge, and water company use
segments.summary: Hosts discuss that randomized experiments found dowsers no better than chance, that James Randi offered a million dollars for proof of paranormal ability, and that UK water companies still use dowsers (per Sally Lapage's investigation). They question why geologists cannot reliably find water and mention seismic and shotgun-based tools.

segments.title: Religious objections to dowsing
segments.summary: Chuck recalls that Christians often considered water witching demonic or folk magic, noting Martin Luther's disapproval and Johann Gottfried Ziegler's book warning against dowsing as tapping into a world spirit.

segments.title: Listener mail from Emily Kenyon
segments.summary: Emily Kenyon from Leicestershire, England writes about how the show has influenced her life: breakfast-for-tea episode, Radium Girls book, water Shed fried chicken recipe, and cleaner house.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Sign-off, with a prompt for listeners to email the show about their geology experience and how the show has affected them.
